claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is compositionally complex and single-phase, with a homogeneous microstructure.
Controlled thermal aging and cyclic mechanical loading can simulate relevant service conditions.
The selected elevated-temperature and cyclic-stress regime provides sufficient atomic mobility for chemical redistribution.
Chemical redistribution can occur under the proposed conditions without large-scale grain growth.
Thermal exposure and cyclic stress drive selected alloying elements to segregate at grain boundaries.
Local chemical variations and stress concentrations are the drivers of grain-boundary segregation.
Grain-boundary segregation mediates local short-range chemical order.
Grain-boundary segregation may nucleate transient nanometer-scale intergranular precipitates.
The localized grain-boundary chemical change reduces grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion facilitates brittle intergranular failure.
Thermally aged and cyclically loaded samples will have lower toughness than the as-synthesized baseline.
The toughness reduction will occur without significant grain coarsening.
The treated alloy will retain an overall single-phase character despite the proposed grain-boundary changes.
Atom probe tomography should reveal greater grain-boundary segregation in treated samples than in ambient controls.
Atom probe tomography may reveal nanometer-scale precipitates in treated samples.
The proposed degradation mechanism applies under moderate-to-high temperatures, cyclic loading, and extended exposure, but outside a substantial grain-coarsening regime.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis permits nanometer-scale intergranular precipitates while also stating that the alloy remains single-phase. A distinct precipitate is ordinarily a second phase, so the intended meaning of 'overall single-phase character' requires clarification, such as allowing a very small secondary-phase fraction below a stated detection limit.
